title: Eigenvalues, Eigenvectors & Diagonalization (5.1-5.2)
description: Covers Days 30-32: the geometric meaning of eigenvectors, the characteristic-polynomial method, the eigenvalue/invertibility connection, complex eigenvalues, similar matrices, the diagonalization theorem, algebraic/geometric multiplicity, defective matrices, and a spectral-decomposition preview for symmetric matrices. 15 questions pulled per attempt from a pool of 80.

questions.prompt: A nonzero vector $v$ is called an eigenvector of $A$ if $Av$ equals _____ for some scalar $\lambda$.
questions.explanation: That's the definition: $Av = \lambda v$ — A can only stretch, shrink, or flip an eigenvector, never rotate it off its own line.

questions.prompt: An eigenvalue of a matrix can be zero.
explanations: An eigenvalue of 0 means $Av=0$ has a nonzero solution — i.e. A is singular. That's completely allowed.

questions.prompt: An eigenvector of $A$ can be the zero vector.
explanations: By definition, eigenvectors must be nonzero — otherwise $A\mathbf{0}=\lambda\mathbf{0}$ would be true for every $\lambda$, which is meaningless.

questions.prompt: Geometrically, if $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ with eigenvalue $\lambda = -1$, what happens to $v$ under the transformation?
choices: v flips to point the opposite direction, same length
v is projected onto a line
explanations: Rotation isn't possible for an eigenvector — it must stay on its own line.
Projection isn't what λ=-1 means.
λ=-1 means it flips direction, not that nothing happens (that would be λ=1).

questions.prompt: If $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ with $Av = 5v$, and $v$ has length 2, what is the length of $Av$?
questions.explanation: Scaling by 5 multiplies the length by 5: 5 × 2 = 10.

questions.prompt: Which best describes what an eigenvalue $\lambda = 0$ tells you about $A$?
choices: A maps some nonzero vector to the zero vector (A is singular)
explanations: λ=0 is a perfectly real eigenvalue.
The identity matrix has eigenvalue 1, not 0.
λ=0 means A is NOT invertible.

questions.prompt: For $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, is $(1,0)$ an eigenvector?
explanations: $A(1,0) = (2,0) = 2\cdot(1,0)$ — it IS an eigenvector, with $\lambda=2$.

questions.prompt: For the same $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, is $(1,1)$ an eigenvector?
explanations: $A(1,1) = (2,1)$, which is NOT a scalar multiple of $(1,1)$ — not an eigenvector.

questions.prompt: For the reflection $A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$, is $(1,-1)$ an eigenvector?
explanations: $A(1,-1) = (-1,1) = -1\cdot(1,-1)$ — it IS an eigenvector, with $\lambda=-1$.

questions.prompt: For the shear $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, is $(0,1)$ an eigenvector?
explanations: $A(0,1) = (1,1)$, which is NOT a scalar multiple of $(0,1)$ — not an eigenvector.

questions.prompt: For the rotation $A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$, is there ANY nonzero real eigenvector?
explanations: A 90° rotation sends every nonzero vector to a new direction — there's no real eigenvector at all (its eigenvalues are complex).

questions.prompt: For the triangular matrix $A = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 3 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$, state both eigenvalues WITHOUT computing a determinant.
questions.explanation: Triangular matrices have their eigenvalues sitting right on the diagonal: 5 and -1.

questions.prompt: To find the eigenvalues of $A$, we solve $\det(A - \lambda I) = $ _____.
questions.explanation: Eigenvalues are exactly the values of λ that make $A-\lambda I$ singular, i.e. $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$.

questions.prompt: Once you know an eigenvalue $\lambda$, how do you find its eigenvector(s)?
explanations: That would only find eigenvectors for λ=0.
The inverse doesn't directly give eigenvectors.
The determinant of A alone doesn't find eigenvectors for a specific λ.

questions.prompt: The eigenvalues of a triangular matrix are exactly its diagonal entries.
explanations: det(A−λI) for a triangular matrix is just the product of (diagonal entry − λ) terms, so the roots are the diagonal entries.

questions.prompt: A $2\times 2$ matrix has trace 9. If one eigenvalue is 7, what is the other?
questions.explanation: The trace of a matrix equals the sum of its eigenvalues: 9 − 7 = 2.

questions.prompt: A $2\times 2$ matrix has $\det(A) = 14$. If one eigenvalue is 7, what is the other?
questions.explanation: The determinant equals the product of the eigenvalues: 14 ÷ 7 = 2.

questions.prompt: Find both eigenvalues of $A = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$.
For the same $A = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$, find an eigenvector for $\lambda=7$.
For the same $A$, find an eigenvector for $\lambda=2$.
Find both eigenvalues of $A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$.
questions.explanation: det(A−λI) = λ²−4 = 0, so λ = 2 or -2.

questions.prompt: Find both eigenvalues of $A = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & -2 \\ 4 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$.
For $A = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & -2 \\ 4 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ and eigenvalue $\lambda=3$, which is a valid eigenvector?
explanations: Check: A(2,1) = (12,9), not a multiple of (2,1).
Check: A(1,-2)=(11,2), not a multiple of (1,-2).
Check: A(3,1)=(19,13), not a multiple of (3,1).

questions.prompt: Find both eigenvalues of $A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$ (today's non-symmetric worked example).
Every real $2\times 2$ matrix has at least one real eigenvalue.
explanations: The rotation matrix $\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}$ has NO real eigenvalues — only the complex pair $\pm i$.

questions.prompt: For symmetric $A=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$, its eigenvectors $(1,1)$ and $(1,-1)$ are orthogonal.
explanations: Their dot product is $1(1)+1(-1)=0$, so yes — orthogonal.

questions.prompt: Which property of a matrix guarantees eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues come out orthogonal?
explanations: Triangular matrices don't guarantee orthogonal eigenvectors.
Invertibility is unrelated to orthogonality of eigenvectors.
Positive diagonal entries don't guarantee this either.

questions.prompt: A non-symmetric matrix's eigenvectors are never orthogonal.
explanations: They CAN happen to be orthogonal, but it's not guaranteed the way it is for symmetric matrices.

questions.prompt: By the extended Invertibility Theorem, $A$ is invertible if and only if _____ is not an eigenvalue of $A$.
questions.explanation: A is singular exactly when det(A)=det(A−0·I)=0, i.e. when 0 is a root of the characteristic polynomial — an eigenvalue.

questions.prompt: If $\det(A) = 0$, then 0 must be an eigenvalue of $A$.
explanations: det(A) = det(A − 0·I), so det(A)=0 means 0 solves the characteristic equation.

questions.prompt: A matrix with eigenvalues 3, -2, and 5 is invertible.
explanations: None of its eigenvalues are 0, so by the theorem it's invertible.

questions.prompt: A matrix with eigenvalues 4, 0, and 6 is invertible.
explanations: 0 is one of its eigenvalues, so the matrix is singular (not invertible).

questions.prompt: A $3\times 3$ matrix has eigenvalues 3, 5, and 7. What is $\det(A)$?
questions.explanation: The determinant equals the product of all eigenvalues: 3 × 5 × 7 = 105.

questions.prompt: Which of these is equivalent to '$A$ is singular (not invertible)'?
choices: every eigenvalue of A is positive
explanations: Positive eigenvalues would actually guarantee invertibility.
Complex eigenvalues don't imply singularity — a rotation matrix is still invertible.
Symmetric matrices can be invertible or not; symmetry alone doesn't decide it.

questions.prompt: For $A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$ with eigenvalues 5 and 2, is $A$ invertible?
explanations: Neither eigenvalue is 0, so A IS invertible.

questions.prompt: Find all eigenvalues of $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$.
questions.explanation: A is triangular, so its eigenvalues are just its diagonal entries: 2, 3, and -1.

questions.prompt: A $3\times 3$ matrix can have a repeated eigenvalue and still be diagonalizable.
explanations: As long as the repeated eigenvalue still has enough independent eigenvectors (geometric multiplicity = algebraic multiplicity), it's fine — more on this Day 32.

questions.prompt: For $A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix}$, how many linearly independent eigenvectors correspond to $\lambda=4$?
explanations: There are actually 2 independent directions — $e_1$ and $e_2$ both work.
Only $e_1$ and $e_2$ correspond to λ=4; $e_3$ belongs to λ=-2.
λ=4 definitely has eigenvectors — it's a genuine eigenvalue here.

questions.prompt: For the same diagonal matrix above, what is the algebraic multiplicity of $\lambda=4$ (how many times it's a root of the characteristic polynomial)?
questions.explanation: The characteristic polynomial is $(\lambda-4)^2(\lambda+2)$, so λ=4 is a double root.

questions.prompt: For a matrix with a repeated eigenvalue, the number of independent eigenvectors for that eigenvalue can be LESS than its multiplicity.
explanations: This is exactly the 'defective' situation — Day 32 gives it a name and works through an example (the Day 30 shear matrix).

questions.prompt: A $3\times 3$ matrix's characteristic polynomial is $(\lambda-2)(\lambda-3)(\lambda+1)$. List its eigenvalues.
questions.explanation: The eigenvalues are the roots of the characteristic polynomial: 2, 3, and -1.

questions.prompt: A $3\times 3$ matrix's characteristic polynomial always has degree...
explanations: Degree matches the matrix size, not 2.
It's not the square of the size.
A degree-1 polynomial would only give one eigenvalue at most, and only for a 1×1 matrix.

questions.prompt: If a real matrix has a complex eigenvalue, its complex conjugate is also an eigenvalue.
explanations: Complex eigenvalues of a REAL matrix always come in conjugate pairs $a\pm bi$.

questions.prompt: If $\lambda = a+bi$ is an eigenvalue of a real matrix, its 'partner' eigenvalue must be _____.
questions.explanation: Complex eigenvalues of a real matrix always occur as conjugate pairs.

questions.prompt: Find the eigenvalues of $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$.
Find the eigenvalues of $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -4 \\ 4 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$.
Geometrically, a real $2\times 2$ matrix with complex eigenvalues represents a transformation that...
choices: rotates (possibly combined with scaling), with no real invariant direction
explanations: A reflection has real eigenvalues (±1).
A projection has real eigenvalues (0 and 1).
A shear has real (repeated) eigenvalues.

questions.prompt: Complex eigenvalues can occur for real matrices, but the corresponding eigenvectors will also involve complex numbers.
explanations: You can't find a real vector satisfying $Av=\lambda v$ for a non-real λ, so the eigenvector must have complex entries too.

questions.prompt: The rotation matrix $\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}$ has eigenvalues...
explanations: Those would be real eigenvalues, which this rotation doesn't have.
The eigenvalues aren't 0 — det(A)=1≠0.
Every matrix has eigenvalues; they're just complex here.

questions.prompt: $B$ is similar to $A$ if there exists an invertible matrix $P$ such that $B = $ _____.
questions.explanation: That's the definition of matrix similarity.

questions.prompt: Similar matrices always have the same eigenvalues.
explanations: Similarity preserves the characteristic polynomial, so the eigenvalues (with multiplicities) match exactly.

questions.prompt: Similar matrices always have the same eigenVECTORS.
explanations: The eigenVALUES match, but the eigenVECTORS transform by P — they're generally different unless P is special.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT guaranteed to be the same for two similar matrices?
explanations: Eigenvalues ARE preserved by similarity.
Determinant IS preserved (det(P⁻¹AP)=det(A)).
Trace IS preserved by similarity too.

questions.prompt: Similar matrices always have the same determinant.
explanations: det(P⁻¹AP) = det(P⁻¹)det(A)det(P) = det(A), since det(P⁻¹)det(P)=1.

questions.prompt: If $A = PDP^{-1}$ with $D$ diagonal, then $A^k$ equals...
explanations: The P's don't get raised to the power — only D does; the middle P's cancel each step.
You can't drop the P's — A itself isn't diagonal.
That reverses the roles of P and P⁻¹.

questions.prompt: If $D = \text{diag}(2,3)$, what is $D^4$?
questions.explanation: Powers of a diagonal matrix just power each diagonal entry: 2⁴=16, 3⁴=81.

questions.prompt: The main computational advantage of diagonalizing $A=PDP^{-1}$ is...
choices: computing high powers of A becomes easy (just power the diagonal entries)
explanations: Diagonalization doesn't change whether A is symmetric.
The determinant is whatever it already was — diagonalizing doesn't change it.
A matrix can be diagonalizable and still have complex eigenvalues.

questions.prompt: Only symmetric matrices can be diagonalized.
explanations: Plenty of non-symmetric matrices are diagonalizable too (e.g. any matrix with distinct eigenvalues) — symmetric ones are just GUARANTEED to be, with orthogonal P.

questions.prompt: Every diagonalizable $n\times n$ matrix has $n$ linearly independent eigenvectors.
explanations: That's exactly what diagonalizability means — enough independent eigenvectors to form a basis (the columns of P).

questions.prompt: $A$ is diagonalizable if and only if, for every eigenvalue, its geometric multiplicity equals its _____ multiplicity.
questions.explanation: That's the Diagonalization Theorem.

questions.prompt: Algebraic multiplicity of an eigenvalue $\lambda$ is...
choices: how many times λ is a root of the characteristic polynomial
the dimension of the eigenspace for λ
explanations: That's the definition of GEOMETRIC multiplicity, not algebraic.
Multiplicity is a count, not the eigenvalue's value.
Multiplicity is about one specific eigenvalue, not the whole matrix's size.

questions.prompt: Geometric multiplicity of an eigenvalue $\lambda$ is...
choices: the dimension of the eigenspace null(A−λI)
how many times λ is a root of the characteristic polynomial
explanations: That's ALGEBRAIC multiplicity.
The trace is unrelated to a single eigenvalue's multiplicity.
It varies — sometimes 1, sometimes matches the algebraic multiplicity, sometimes in between.

questions.prompt: Geometric multiplicity can never exceed algebraic multiplicity.
explanations: You can never have MORE independent eigenvectors for λ than λ's multiplicity as a root — geometric ≤ algebraic always.

questions.prompt: A matrix with $n$ distinct eigenvalues ($n\times n$) is automatically diagonalizable.
explanations: Distinct eigenvalues always come with independent eigenvectors, so geometric = algebraic = 1 for each — the theorem's condition is automatically satisfied.

questions.prompt: A matrix with a repeated eigenvalue can never be diagonalized.
explanations: It CAN still be diagonalized, as long as that eigenvalue's geometric multiplicity matches its algebraic multiplicity (e.g. any diagonal matrix with a repeated entry).

questions.prompt: A square matrix that is NOT diagonalizable is called _____.
questions.explanation: That's the standard term for a non-diagonalizable matrix.

questions.prompt: For the shear $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, $\lambda=1$ has algebraic multiplicity 2. What is its geometric multiplicity?
questions.explanation: null(A−I) = null([[0,1],[0,0]]) is only 1-dimensional (spanned by (1,0)) — geometric multiplicity 1 < algebraic multiplicity 2, so A is defective.

questions.prompt: The shear matrix from Day 30 is defective.
explanations: Its repeated eigenvalue λ=1 has only 1 independent eigenvector instead of the 2 its algebraic multiplicity would need — that's the definition of defective.

questions.prompt: Which of these matrices is defective?
explanations: This is already diagonal — its repeated eigenvalue 4 has 2 independent eigenvectors, so it's fine.
Distinct eigenvalues (2 and 3) are automatically fine — not defective.

questions.prompt: $\begin{bmatrix}4&0\\0&4\end{bmatrix}$ (λ=4 with algebraic multiplicity 2) is diagonalizable even though its eigenvalue is repeated.
explanations: It's already diagonal, so its geometric multiplicity is 2, matching its algebraic multiplicity — perfectly diagonalizable (it IS D already).

questions.prompt: For $A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$ with eigenvalues 5 (eigenvector (1,1)) and 2 (eigenvector (1,-2)), what is $D$ in $A=PDP^{-1}$ (matching column order $P=[(1,1),(1,-2)]$)?
questions.explanation: D's diagonal entries are the eigenvalues, in the same order as their eigenvectors appear as columns of P.

questions.prompt: Using the same $A$, with $P$'s columns being the eigenvectors $(1,1)$ and $(1,-2)$ in that order, what is $P$?
explanations: The rows are swapped from the correct eigenvector columns.
That's D, not P.
That's the original matrix A, not P.

questions.prompt: Once $A=PDP^{-1}$ is proposed, you can check your work by verifying $AP=PD$ (without ever computing $P^{-1}$).
explanations: Multiplying both sides of A=PDP⁻¹ by P on the right gives AP=PD — an easier check since it avoids computing an inverse.

questions.prompt: For $A=\begin{bmatrix}4&1\\2&3\end{bmatrix}$ diagonalized as above, $A^3$ applied to the eigenvector $(1,1)$ gives what scalar times $(1,1)$?
questions.explanation: Eigenvectors stay eigenvectors under powers of A, with eigenvalue raised to that power: 5³ = 125.

questions.prompt: Compared to a general diagonalization $A=PDP^{-1}$, what's special about a symmetric matrix's decomposition?
choices: P can be chosen orthogonal, so inverting P is free (just transpose)
explanations: D is still diagonal — that part doesn't change.
Symmetric doesn't mean triangular.
Symmetric matrices actually always have REAL eigenvalues, never complex.
